claim: During navigation, the visual responses of neurons in mouse primary visual cortex (V1) are modulated by the animal's spatial position.
source: During navigation, the visual responses of neurons in mouse primary visual cortex (V1) are modulated by the animal's spatial position.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study, supported by experimental data shown in Figures 1-4.

claim: Spatial modulation is similarly present across multiple higher visual areas.
source: Here we show that this spatial modulation is similarly present across multiple higher visual areas but negligible in the main thalamic pathway into V1.
evidence: Supported by experimental data from six higher visual areas shown in Figures 2 and 3.

claim: Spatial modulation is negligible in the main thalamic pathway into V1.
source: Here we show that this spatial modulation is similarly present across multiple higher visual areas but negligible in the main thalamic pathway into V1.
evidence: Supported by experimental data from LGN boutons and neurons shown in Figure 2.

claim: Similar to hippocampus, spatial modulation in visual cortex strengthens with experience.
source: Similar to hippocampus, spatial modulation in visual cortex strengthens with experience and with active behavior.
evidence: Supported by experimental data across days shown in Figure 1e-h, and comparison to hippocampal literature.

claim: Spatial modulation in visual cortex strengthens with active behavior.
source: Similar to hippocampus, spatial modulation in visual cortex strengthens with experience and with active behavior.
evidence: Supported by experimental data comparing VR to replay conditions shown in Figure 4.

claim: Active navigation in a familiar environment enhances the spatial modulation of visual signals starting in the cortex.
source: Active navigation in a familiar environment, therefore, enhances the spatial modulation of visual signals starting in the cortex.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion drawn from the combined findings about experience, active behavior, and cortical vs. thalamic modulation.

claim: The activity of mouse primary visual cortex (V1) is influenced by navigational signals.
source: There is increasing evidence that the activity of the mouse primary visual cortex (V1) is influenced by navigational signals (Fiser et al., 2016; Flossmann and Rochefort, 2021; Fournier et al., 2020; Haggerty and Ji, 2015; Ji and Wilson, 2007; Pakan et al., 2018; Saleem et al., 2018).
evidence: Supported by multiple citations to previous literature.

claim: During navigation, the visual responses of V1 neurons are modulated by the animal's estimate of spatial position.
source: During navigation, indeed, the visual responses of V1 neurons are modulated by the animal's estimate of spatial position (Saleem et al., 2018).
evidence: Supported by citation to previous work.

claim: The underlying spatial signals in V1 covary with those in hippocampus.
source: The underlying spatial signals covary with those in hippocampus and are affected similarly by idiothetic cues (Fournier et al., 2020; Saleem et al., 2018).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous work.

claim: Spatial signals in V1 are affected similarly to hippocampus by idiothetic cues.
source: The underlying spatial signals covary with those in hippocampus and are affected similarly by idiothetic cues (Fournier et al., 2020; Saleem et al., 2018).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous work.

claim: Spatial signals have been seen in thalamus.
source: Indeed, spatial signals have been seen elsewhere in thalamus (Jankowski et al., 2015; Taube, 1995) and possibly also in LGN itself (Hok et al., 2018).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous work.

claim: Spatial signals have possibly been seen in LGN itself.
source: Indeed, spatial signals have been seen elsewhere in thalamus (Jankowski et al., 2015; Taube, 1995) and possibly also in LGN itself (Hok et al., 2018).
evidence: Supported by citation to previous work, with qualification 'possibly'.

claim: Many neurons in parietal cortex are associated with spatial coding.
source: For instance, they might be stronger in parietal areas such as A and AM (Hovde et al., 2018), because many neurons in parietal cortex are associated with spatial coding (Krumin et al., 2018; McNaughton et al., 1994; Nitz, 2006; Save and Poucet, 2009; Whitlock et al., 2012; Wilber et al., 2014).
evidence: Supported by multiple citations to previous literature.

claim: In the navigational system, spatial encoding is stronger in active navigation than during passive viewing.
source: In the navigational system, spatial encoding is stronger in active navigation than during passive viewing, when most hippocampal place cells lose their place fields (Chen et al., 2013; Song et al., 2005; Terrazas et al., 2005).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous work on hippocampus.

claim: Most hippocampal place cells lose their place fields during passive viewing.
source: In the navigational system, spatial encoding is stronger in active navigation than during passive viewing, when most hippocampal place cells lose their place fields (Chen et al., 2013; Song et al., 2005; Terrazas et al., 2005).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous work.

claim: Hippocampal place fields grow stronger when an environment becomes familiar.
source: In addition, both hippocampal place fields and entorhinal grid patterns grow stronger when an environment becomes familiar (Barry et al., 2012; Frank et al., 2004; Karlsson and Frank, 2008).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous work.

claim: Entorhinal grid patterns grow stronger when an environment becomes familiar.
source: In addition, both hippocampal place fields and entorhinal grid patterns grow stronger when an environment becomes familiar (Barry et al., 2012; Frank et al., 2004; Karlsson and Frank, 2008).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous work.

claim: V1 neurons tended to respond to the visual patterns more strongly at a single location.
source: V1 neurons tended to respond to the visual patterns more strongly at a single location (Fournier et al., 2020; Saleem et al., 2018; Figure 1b)
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1b and citations to previous work.

claim: The preferred locations of V1 neurons were broadly distributed along the corridor.
source: and their preferred locations were broadly distributed along the corridor (Figure 1c, Figure 1—figure supplement 1a–c).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1c and supplementary figures.

claim: The median SMI for responsive V1 neurons was 0.39 ± 0.19.
source: The median SMI for responsive V1 neurons was 0.39 ± 0.19 (n = 39 sessions)
evidence: Direct quantitative measurement from experimental data.

claim: 44% of V1 neurons had SMI > 0.5.
source: and 44% of V1 neurons (1322/2992) had SMI > 0.5.
evidence: Direct quantitative measurement from experimental data.

claim: Spatial modulation in V1 grew with experience.
source: Spatial modulation in V1 grew with experience (Figure 1e–h).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1e-h.

claim: The spatial modulation increased with experience and was significantly larger on day 5 compared to day 1.
source: Indeed, the spatial modulation increased with experience and was significantly larger on day 5 compared to day 1 (Figure 1h, median SMI: 0.45 on day 5 vs. 0.24 on day 1; p<10−12, two-sided Wilcoxon rank sum test).
evidence: Supported by experimental data with statistical testing shown in Figure 1h.

claim: Spatial position barely affected the visual responses of LGN afferents in experienced mice.
source: In contrast to V1 neurons, spatial position barely affected the visual responses of LGN afferents in experienced mice (Figure 2a–d).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2a-d.

claim: LGN boutons in layer 4 gave mostly similar visual responses in the two segments of the corridor.
source: LGN boutons in layer 4 gave mostly similar visual responses in the two segments of the corridor (Figure 2b,c)
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2b,c.

claim: The locations where LGN boutons fired clustered around the landmarks as expected from purely visual responses.
source: and the locations where they fired clustered around the landmarks as expected from purely visual responses (Figure 1—figure supplement 1e).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in supplementary figure.

claim: The spatial modulation in LGN boutons was small.
source: The spatial modulation in LGN boutons was small (Figure 2d), with a median SMI barely above zero (median ± m.a.d.: 0.07 ± 0.05, n = 19 sessions).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2d.

claim: The median SMI of LGN boutons was slightly positive.
source: It was slightly positive (p=0.002, right-tailed Wilcoxon signed rank test)
evidence: Supported by statistical testing of experimental data.

claim: The SMI of LGN boutons was markedly smaller than the SMIs of V1 neurons.
source: but markedly smaller than the SMIs of V1 neurons (p=10−6, left-tailed Wilcoxon rank sum test).
evidence: Supported by statistical comparison of experimental data.

claim: Only 4% of LGN boutons had SMI > 0.5, compared to 44% in V1.
source: Only 4% of LGN boutons (37/840) had SMI > 0.5, compared to 44% in V1.
evidence: Direct quantitative comparison from experimental data.

claim: Among LGN boutons with SMI > 0.5, most (28/37) fired more strongly in the first half of the corridor.
source: Moreover, among these few neurons, most (28/37) fired more strongly in the first half of the corridor (Figure 1—figure supplement 1f), as might be expected from contrast adaptation mechanisms (Dhruv and Carandini, 2014).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in supplementary figure and citation to contrast adaptation literature.

claim: LGN units gave responses and SMI similar to LGN boutons.
source: LGN units gave responses and SMI similar to LGN boutons (median ± m.a.d.: 0.06 ± 0.02, p=0.78, Wilcoxon rank sum test).
evidence: Supported by experimental data from electrophysiology recordings with statistical comparison.

claim: The median SMI of LGN units was slightly positive.
source: Median SMI was slightly positive (p=0.03, right-tailed Wilcoxon signed rank test)
evidence: Supported by statistical testing of experimental data.

claim: The median SMI of LGN units was markedly smaller than in V1.
source: but again markedly smaller than in V1 (p=0.002, left-tailed Wilcoxon rank sum test).
evidence: Supported by statistical comparison of experimental data.

claim: Spatial modulation was broadly similar across HVAs and not significantly larger than in V1.
source: Spatial modulation was broadly similar across HVAs and not significantly larger than in V1 (Figure 2e–h, Figure 3).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figures 2 and 3.

claim: Pooling across six higher visual areas, the median SMI across sessions was 0.40 ± 0.12.
source: Pooling across these areas, the median SMI across sessions was 0.40 ± 0.12, significantly larger than zero (n = 52 sessions, p=10−10, right-tailed Wilcoxon signed rank test, Figure 2h)
evidence: Direct quantitative measurement from experimental data with statistical testing.

claim: The median SMI of HVAs was not significantly different from V1.
source: and not significantly different from V1 (Wilcoxon rank sum test: p=0.88).
evidence: Supported by statistical comparison of experimental data.

claim: Spatial modulation was present in each of the six higher visual areas.
source: Spatial modulation was present in each of the six areas (Figure 3)
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3.

claim: Spatial modulation in visual areas was not affected by reward protocol or mouse line.
source: and, as in V1, was not affected by reward protocol or mouse line (Figure 3—figure supplement 3).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in supplementary figure.

claim: Spatial modulation could not be explained by other factors such as running speed, reward events, pupil size, and eye position.
source: In addition, spatial modulation could not be explained by other factors such as running speed, reward events, pupil size, and eye position (Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Supported by modeling analysis shown in supplementary figure.

claim: In V1, spatial modulation was larger in neurons with central rather than peripheral receptive fields.
source: In V1, spatial modulation was larger in neurons with central rather than peripheral receptive fields (Figure 3—figure supplement 2) irrespective of mouse line or reward protocol (Figure 3—figure supplement 3).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in supplementary figures.

claim: A similar trend of lower SMI in periphery-biased areas was seen across higher areas.
source: A similar trend was seen across higher areas, with slightly lower SMI in areas biased toward the periphery (AM, PM) (Garrett et al., 2014; Wang and Burkhalter, 2007; Zhuang et al., 2017) than in areas biased toward the central visual field (LM, RL, Figure 3c).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3c and citations to retinotopic organization literature.

claim: During 'running replay' the baseline activity of LGN boutons decreased slightly.
source: During 'running replay' the baseline activity of LGN boutons decreased slightly (Figure 4a,b, Figure 4—figure supplement 1a, p=0.003, paired-sample right-tailed t-test).
evidence: Supported by experimental data with statistical testing shown in Figure 4.

claim: The median SMI of LGN boutons in 'running replay' remained a mere 0.05 ± 0.06.
source: However, the median SMI in 'running replay' remained a mere 0.05 ± 0.06 (n = 18 sessions), not significantly different from the 0.08 ± 0.05 measured in VR (Figure 4b, p=0.29, Wilcoxon signed rank test).
evidence: Direct quantitative measurement from experimental data with statistical testing.

claim: During stationary replay, baseline activity of LGN boutons decreased markedly.
source: Similar results were obtained during stationary replay (Figure 4c,d): baseline activity decreased markedly (Erisken et al., 2014) (p=10−65 paired-sample right-tailed t-test, Figure 4—figure supplement 1b)
evidence: Supported by experimental data with statistical testing and citation to previous work.

claim: The median SMI of LGN boutons during stationary replay remained negligible at 0.03 ± 0.04.
source: but the median SMI remained negligible at 0.03 ± 0.04 and not different from the 0.07 ± 0.04 measured in VR (n = 18 sessions, p=0.053, Wilcoxon signed rank test, Figure 4d).
evidence: Direct quantitative measurement from experimental data with statistical testing.

claim: Many V1 neurons showed weaker modulation by spatial position during replay than in VR, particularly during stationary replay.
source: Many V1 neurons showed weaker modulation by spatial position during replay than in VR, particularly during stationary replay (Figure 4e–h).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4e-h.

claim: In V1, 'running replay' reduced median SMI by ~10%, from 0.42 ± 0.15 in VR to 0.38 ± 0.14.
source: In V1, 'running replay' reduced median SMI by ~10%, from 0.42 ± 0.15 in VR to 0.38 ± 0.14 (n = 32 sessions, p=0.01, right-tailed Wilcoxon signed rank test, Figure 4e,f).
evidence: Direct quantitative measurement from experimental data with statistical testing.

claim: The decrease in spatial modulation during running replay was not associated with mean activity differences in V1.
source: This decrease in spatial modulation was not associated with mean activity differences (p>0.05, paired-sample right-tailed t-test, Figure 4—figure supplement 1a).
evidence: Supported by statistical testing of experimental data shown in supplementary figure.

claim: Running without matched visual feedback did not result in the same spatial modulation as active navigation.
source: Therefore, running without matched visual feedback did not result in the same spatial modulation as active navigation.
evidence: Inference drawn from the comparison of VR and running replay conditions.

claim: During stationary replay in V1, activity decreased markedly.
source: As expected in mice that are not running (Keller et al., 2012; Saleem et al., 2013), activity decreased markedly (p=10−24, paired-sample right-tailed t-test, Figure 4—figure supplement 1b).
evidence: Supported by experimental data with statistical testing and citations to previous work.

claim: In V1, the median SMI halved from 0.38 ± 0.21 in VR to 0.18 ± 0.12 in stationary replay.
source: In addition, the median SMI halved from 0.38 ± 0.21 in VR to 0.18 ± 0.12 in stationary replay, a significant decrease (n = 24 sessions, p=0.005, right-tailed Wilcoxon signed rank test).
evidence: Direct quantitative measurement from experimental data with statistical testing.

claim: In HVAs, 'running replay' reduced median SMI by ~33%, from 0.40 ± 0.10 in VR to 0.27 ± 0.10.
source: Here, 'running replay' reduced median SMI by ~33%, from 0.40 ± 0.10 in VR to 0.27 ± 0.10 (n = 41 sessions, p=10−6, right-tailed Wilcoxon signed rank test, Figure 4i,j)
evidence: Direct quantitative measurement from experimental data with statistical testing.

claim: The decrease in SMI during running replay in HVAs was without affecting overall activity.
source: without affecting overall activity (p>0.05 in all areas, paired-sample right-tailed t-test, Figure 4—figure supplement 1a).
evidence: Supported by statistical testing of experimental data shown in supplementary figure.

claim: In HVAs during stationary replay, the median SMI decreased ~68%, from 0.34 ± 0.15 in VR to 0.11 ± 0.11.
source: Even stronger effects were seen during stationary replay (Figure 4k,l), where the median SMI decreased ~68%, from 0.34 ± 0.15 in VR to 0.11 ± 0.11 (n = 33 sessions, p=10−6, right-tailed Wilcoxon signed rank test, Figure 4k,l).
evidence: Direct quantitative measurement from experimental data with statistical testing.

claim: The decrease in SMI during stationary replay in HVAs was accompanied by decreased firing in some areas, notably AM and PM.
source: This effect was accompanied by decreased firing in some areas, notably AM (p=0.03) and PM (p=10−9, paired-sample right-tailed t-test, Figure 4—figure supplement 1b).
evidence: Supported by statistical testing of experimental data shown in supplementary figure.

claim: Upon experience active navigation modulates the amplitude of visual responses along the visual pathway and does so primarily in the cortex.
source: Taken together, these results indicate that upon experience active navigation modulates the amplitude of visual responses along the visual pathway and does so primarily in the cortex.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion drawn from all the experimental findings.

claim: The spatial modulation of V1 visual responses strengthened across the first days of experience.
source: This spatial modulation of V1 visual responses strengthened across the first days of experience, perhaps more slowly than the development of navigational signals in hippocampus (Frank et al., 2004; Karlsson and Frank, 2008) but similar to retrosplenial cortex (Mao et al., 2018).
evidence: Supported by experimental data and comparison to cited literature.

claim: Similar results have been observed when decoding spatial position from V1 across days of exposure to a slightly changing environment.
source: Similar results have been observed when decoding spatial position from V1 across days of exposure to a slightly changing environment (Fiser et al., 2016).
evidence: Supported by citation to previous work.

claim: The spatial modulation of V1 responses is unlikely to be inherited from LGN.
source: The spatial modulation of V1 responses is unlikely to be inherited from LGN, because this modulation was negligible in LGN inputs to layer 4 and in LGN neurons themselves (regardless of what layer they project to Cruz-Martín et al., 2014).
evidence: Inference drawn from experimental data showing negligible LGN modulation, with citation to LGN projection literature.

claim: The mice were head restrained and hence lacked vestibular inputs.
source: However, our mice were head restrained and hence lacked vestibular inputs, which may be relevant (Ravassard et al., 2013; Russell et al., 2006).
evidence: Direct statement about experimental conditions with citations to vestibular input literature.

claim: Perhaps when mice freely move, LGN does show some spatial modulation.
source: Perhaps when mice freely move, LGN does show some spatial modulation (Hok et al., 2018), which is possibly amplified in V1 by nonlinear mechanisms (Chariker et al., 2016; Lien and Scanziani, 2013).
evidence: Speculative statement with citations to relevant literature.

claim: Spatial modulation affected all cortical visual areas approximately equally.
source: Spatial modulation affected all cortical visual areas approximately equally, consistent with the widespread neural coding of task-related information across the posterior cortex (Koay et al., 2021; Minderer et al., 2019).
evidence: Supported by experimental data and citations to literature on task-related coding.

claim: All cortical visual areas gave stronger visual responses during active behavior than during passive viewing.
source: In addition, all areas gave stronger visual responses during active behavior than during passive viewing.
evidence: Supported by experimental data comparing VR to replay conditions.

claim: Navigational signals may reach visual cortex through retrosplenial cortex.
source: Navigational signals may reach visual cortex through retrosplenial cortex (Makino and Komiyama, 2015), an area that contains experience-dependent spatial signals (Mao et al., 2017; Mao et al., 2018), and is more strongly modulated by active navigation than V1 (Fischer et al., 2020).
evidence: Speculative statement with citations to relevant literature.

claim: Another candidate source of navigational signals is anterior cingulate cortex.
source: Another candidate is anterior cingulate cortex (Zhang et al., 2014), whose dense projections to V1 carry signals related to locomotion (Leinweber et al., 2017).
evidence: Speculative statement with citations to relevant literature.

claim: The route that navigational signals take across the cortex is yet to be charted.
source: The route that navigational signals take across the cortex is yet to be charted.
evidence: Statement about current knowledge gap.

claim: The virtual corridor was 8 cm wide and 100 cm long.
source: Briefly, the corridor was 8 cm wide and 100 cm long.
evidence: Direct description of experimental methods.

claim: A vertical grating or a plaid, 8 cm wide each, alternated in the sequence grating-plaid-grating-plaid at 20, 40, 60, and 80 cm from the start of the corridor.
source: A vertical grating or a plaid, 8 cm wide each, alternated in the sequence grating-plaid-grating-plaid at 20, 40, 60, and 80 cm from the start of the corridor.
evidence: Direct description of experimental methods.

claim: The virus could infect neighboring thalamic nuclei, including the higher-order visual thalamic nucleus LP.
source: In addition to dorsal LGN, the virus could infect neighboring thalamic nuclei, including the higher-order visual thalamic nucleus LP, which projects to layer 1 of visual cortex (Roth et al., 2016).
evidence: Statement about potential experimental confound with citation to projection literature.

claim: Boutons were imaged only in layer 4, the main recipient of dorsal LGN inputs.
source: Therefore, we imaged boutons only in layer 4, the main recipient of dorsal LGN inputs.
evidence: Statement about experimental design based on anatomical knowledge.

claim: Calcium traces were deconvolved, yielding inferred firing rates.
source: To estimate activity, the calcium traces were deconvolved, yielding inferred firing rates (Pachitariu et al., 2016a; Pachitariu et al., 2018).
evidence: Description of data processing method with citations.

claim: A purely visual neuron would respond to visual patterns similarly in both segments.
source: A purely visual neuron would respond to visual patterns similarly in both segments, while a neuron modulated by spatial position could respond more strongly in one segment.
evidence: Logical inference about expected neural responses based on experimental design.

claim: A neuron modulated by spatial position could respond more strongly in one segment.
source: A purely visual neuron would respond to visual patterns similarly in both segments, while a neuron modulated by spatial position could respond more strongly in one segment.
evidence: Logical inference about expected neural responses based on experimental design.

claim: Visual patterns in the central visual field were further away in the corridor.
source: Visual patterns in the central visual field were further away in the corridor, and thus were likely less effective in driving responses than patterns in the periphery, which were closer to the animal and thus larger.
evidence: Inference about visual stimulus effectiveness based on experimental setup.

claim: Visual patterns in the periphery were closer to the animal and thus larger.
source: Visual patterns in the central visual field were further away in the corridor, and thus were likely less effective in driving responses than patterns in the periphery, which were closer to the animal and thus larger.
evidence: Inference about visual stimulus properties based on experimental setup.

claim: If spatial modulation signals reach visual cortex from the navigational system, they should grow with active navigation and with experience of the environment.
source: If spatial modulation signals reach visual cortex from the navigational system, therefore, they should grow with active navigation and with experience of the environment.
evidence: Logical prediction based on known properties of the navigational system.
